extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students in combinatorics and discrete mathematics; mathematical readers studying combinatorial methods and proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and presents central combinatorial theorems, proof techniques, and example constructions (double counting, extremal graph bounds, Sperner, Erdős–Ko–Rado, Hall, shuffling analyses) as used in a combinatorics textbook. Emphasizes statements, necessary conditions, and typical proof ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting (counting in two ways)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count a set S by two different methods and equate the results (e.g., sum of degrees = 2|E| because every vertex contributes d(v) and every edge has two ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly as a central combinatorial technique: pick a set of combinatorial objects (pairs, incidences, occurrences), count them by summing over one index (e.g., vertices) and independently over another (e.g., edges or pairs), then equate to derive inequalities or exact formulas. Examples in the text include counting pairs (u,{v,w}) to bound edges in C4-free graphs and counting vectors/subspaces in finite geometry constructions. Typical pattern: define S, compute |S| as sum_u f(u), bound |S| by another combinatorial property (e.g., each pair has ≤1 common neighbor), then combine with inequalities (Cauchy–Schwarz) to get numeric bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal bound for graphs without 4-cycles (Reiman's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the graph G on n vertices contains no 4-cycles, then |E| ≤ (1/4) n (1 + sqrt{4n - 3}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by double counting the set S of triples (u,{v,w}) where u adjacent to both v and w (v ≠ w): |S| = Σ_u C(d(u),2). Under the C4 condition, each unordered pair {v,w} has at most one common neighbor, so |S| ≤ C(n,2). Apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the degree vector and solve the resulting quadratic to obtain the stated upper bound. For small n illustrative equality cases are discussed (n=5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Cauchy–Schwarz on degree vectors to bound graph parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to the degree vector (d(u1),...,d(un)) against the all-ones vector to relate Σ d(u)^2 to (Σ d(u))^2 / n, producing bounds linking average degree, sum of squares, and number of edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical step in extremal graph arguments: after obtaining Σ C(d(u),2) or Σ d(u)^2 from double counting, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to lower- or upper-bound these sums in terms of |E| and n. Combine with combinatorial upper bounds (e.g., from forbidden subgraphs) to get numeric inequalities solved by quadratic equations. The text uses this to go from Σ C(d(u),2) to an inequality that yields Reiman's bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-geometry construction of near-extremal C4-free graphs (projective plane over F_p)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct G_p whose vertices are one-dimensional subspaces of the 3-dim vector space over Z_p, with adjacency defined by v·w = 0; this graph has n = p^2 + p + 1 vertices and about (1/2) n (p+1) edges and contains no 4-cycles, nearly attaining Reiman's bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that vertices correspond to projective points, adjacency to polar lines; shows uniqueness of common neighbors (hence C4-free) via linear algebra (solution space dimension 1). Counts vertices and degrees by double counting vectors in subspaces; distinguishes vertices on a conic (degree p) and off-conic (degree p+1). Uses symmetric matrix A of adjacency to analyze eigenvalues and trace, completing the count. This is the standard finite-geometry extremal example approaching the upper bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner's lemma (triangulation coloring condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a triangulated 'big' triangle with vertices V1,V2,V3 and a vertex coloring from {1,2,3} such that each Vi gets color i, vertices along edge ViVj use only colors i and j, and interior vertices arbitrary, then there exists at least one small triangle with all three different vertex colors (a tricolored triangle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger conclusion: the number of tricolored small triangles is odd (hence nonzero). Proof strategy uses a partial dual graph: include only edges crossing edges with endcolors 1 and 2; interior tricolored triangles correspond to vertices of odd degree in this partial dual; the outside dual vertex has odd degree as well, and since finite graphs have an even number of odd-degree vertices, there must be an odd number of interior tricolored triangles. The lemma is presented for n=2 with remarks on extension by induction for higher dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving Brouwer's fixed point theorem from Sperner's lemma (n=2 case)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a sequence of triangulations of the simplex and Sperner colorings induced by a continuous map f to find nested tricolored triangles whose limit point is a fixed point of f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define color X(v) := min{i : (f(v)-v)_i < 0} assuming f has no fixed point (so some coordinate difference must be negative). This coloring satisfies Sperner's boundary conditions (each vertex ei gets color i, edge opposite ei cannot have color i). Apply Sperner to each finer triangulation: get tricolored small triangle; take a convergent subsequence of their vertices as mesh→0. Continuity of f then forces f(v)=v at the limit, contradicting the assumption—so f has a fixed point. The text outlines constructing triangulations with mesh→0 (e.g., barycentric subdivisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sperner's theorem (Lubell's double-counting proof for largest antichain)
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of a largest antichain of an n-set is binomial(n, floor(n/2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lubell's short proof: count maximal chains 0 = C0 ⊂ C1 ⊂ ... ⊂ Cn = N (there are n! such chains). For each A in the antichain of size k, exactly k!(n-k)! chains contain A. Since no chain contains two distinct members of the antichain, summing over the family gives ≤ n!, leading after rearrangement to Σ m_k / C(n,k) ≤ 1 and hence |F| ≤ max_k C(n,k). The text mentions that the families achieving equality are the k-sets for k = floor(n/2) (two families if n odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem and the circle-arc lemma (Katona's proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n ≥ 2k, the largest size of an intersecting family of k-sets of an n-set is C(n-1,k-1) (achieved by all k-sets containing a fixed element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Katona's elegant proof uses a combinatorial lemma about arcs on a circle: given n points on a circle and t distinct arcs of length k (k consecutive points/edges) with any two arcs sharing an edge, then t ≤ k. Use cyclic permutations: for any cyclic permutation, at most k members of the intersecting family can appear as k consecutive numbers; summing over all (n-1)! cyclic permutations and counting multiplicities yields the desired bound. The lemma's proof rests on endpoint-counting and the assumption n ≥ 2k. Edge cases (n=2k and small n) are discussed and exceptions characterized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's marriage theorem (SDR existence condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection A1,...,An of subsets of a finite set X admits a system of distinct representatives (SDR) if and only if for every m (1 ≤ m ≤ n) the union of any m of the Ai contains at least m elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The necessity is immediate (m sets cannot be represented by m distinct elements if their union has < m elements). Sufficiency proven by induction via the concept of a 'critical family' (a subcollection of e sets whose union has size e): either no critical family exists (pick x in A1, remove it and apply induction) or a critical family exists (represent that family by induction on smaller universe, then apply induction to the remaining sets avoiding the chosen representatives). The textbook also frames this as the marriage problem and gives references and further applications in matching theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of k disjoint SDRs under multiplicity constraint (variant of Hall)
rubrics_metrics.description: If each Ai has size k ≥ 1 and no element of the universe is contained in more than k of the Ai, then there exist k SDRs that together give k distinct representatives for every Ai.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as an appealing result left for the reader to prove (a corollary/extension in matching theory). It asserts that one can select k pairwise-disjoint systems of distinct representatives so that for each i the k chosen representatives for Ai are distinct (forming Ai itself as a set of representatives). This is the kind of combinatorial strengthening used in applications of Hall's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birthday paradox probability formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability that n random people all have different birthdays (365-day year, no seasonality) is Π_{i=1}^{n-1} (1 - i/365).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the paradoxical threshold (for example, probability < 1/2 already at n = 23). Analogue: placing n balls independently into K boxes, probability no box gets more than one ball is Π_{i=1}^{n-1} (1 - i/K). Method: view people sequentially and multiply conditional probabilities that each new person avoids previous birthdays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupon collector expectation and tail bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected number of draws to collect all n distinct coupons is n H_n ≈ n log n; and for m = n log n + c n the tail bound Prob[V > m] < e^{-c}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive expectation by summing geometric expectations for time to collect the (k+1)-th new coupon when k are already collected: E = Σ_{i=0}^{n-1} n/(n-i) = n H_n. For tail bounds, use union bound on events 'coupon i not drawn in first m draws' and the inequality (1 - i/n)^m ≤ exp(-i m / n), leading to Prob[V > m] ≤ Σ_i (1 - i/n)^m ≤ exp(-c) for m = n log n + c n. Text gives constant approximations and remarks on harmonic number bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation distance as measure of closeness to uniform distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Variation distance between two probability distributions Q1 and Q2 on the symmetric group S_n is ||Q1 - Q2|| = max_{S ⊆ S_n} |Q1(S) - Q2(S)| = (1/2) Σ_{π ∈ S_n} |Q1(π) - Q2(π)|; used to quantify 'how close to random' a shuffled deck is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text defines starting distribution E (identity) and uniform U, notes that ||E - U|| is close to 1; studies how repeating shuffles reduces variation distance. General Markov-chain theory shows exponential decay but not the 'cutoff' phenomenon; variation distance is the standard (unforgiving) metric in the analysis of shuffling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong uniform stopping rules for shuffling
rubrics_metrics.description: A stopping rule (depending only on observed random shuffles so far) is strong uniform if for every k > 0, conditional on stopping at time T = k, the permutation of the deck is uniformly distributed over S_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: (1) such rules exist for many shuffle models; (2) analyzing Prob[T > k] often reduces to simple combinatorial problems and gives effective upper bounds on variation distance d(k) = ||distribution after k shuffles - U||; (3) example for top-in-at-random shuffles: 'STOP after the original bottom card (labelled n) is first inserted back into the deck'—tracing that card shows uniformity of the order below it at that time. Formal condition: Prob[X_k = π | T = k] = 1/n! for all π ∈ S_n. This links stopping times to strong uniform times and provides practical bounds via tail probabilities of T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-in-at-random shuffle model and its coupon-collector analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Top-in-at-random shuffle: remove top card and insert it into a uniformly random position among n choices. A strong uniform stopping rule is to stop when the original bottom card has been inserted back; analyzing the distribution of the stopping time reduces to successive coupon-collector-type waiting times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the number of steps until i cards lie below the tracked bottom card as T_i; the increments T_i - T_{i-1} correspond to geometric waiting times analogous to coupon collector problems (probability of inserting top card into one of i positions below the tracked card). Summing these gives the stopping time T which can be bounded in expectation and tail probability using coupon-collector estimates, yielding bounds on the variation distance after k shuffles.
